absent: No information about run-queue structure beyond the raw accessor and pinned offset.
No information about context switch, enqueue, dequeue, wakeup, or next-task selection.
No information about mutex or realtime mutex internals or blocking paths.
No information about autogroup, core scheduling, migration target selection, or cache policy beyond empty hooks and layouts.
No information about deadline bandwidth, admission, throttling, or server mechanics beyond predicates.
No information about extension scheduler operations, dispatch iteration, or BPF interaction beyond queue and flag layouts.
No information about tick, scaling, timer expiry, or signal-level accounting beyond inline copies and atomic adds.
No information about clock source, stability detection, or interrupt-time accounting beyond trivial mappings.

findings.text: The scheduler exposes helpers to observe and maintain which mutex a task is currently blocked on. One accessor returns the recorded association, one records a new association, and two clearing forms reset the association to empty, with one clearing form acquiring the guard itself and the inner forms expecting the caller to already hold it.

Access to the blocked-on association is serialized by a per-task guard. All inner observation and mutation helpers require that guard to be held on entry, and the outer clearing helper takes the guard in interrupt-safe mode before delegating.

Recording a blocked-on association is only valid for the running task itself and must not replace a different recorded mutex; repeating the same mutex is accepted. Clearing accepts an empty expectation or a matching mutex but warns when asked to clear a different association.
For the realtime mutex flavor the clear helpers are defined as empty operations that accept a task and a lock but change no state.
A predicate reports whether the current execution context has a pending rescheduling request, delegating to thread flag inspection.

In the multiprocessor variant the current CPU of a task is obtained from associated thread information with single-load semantics, while the single-processor variant always reports zero and provides an empty CPU setter.
A task counts as runnable only while it remains queued on a run queue and is not marked as delayed in its fair scheduling entity.

Lock holder liveness combines two checks: the owner is marked as present on a CPU and that CPU is not reported as preempted by the virtualization helper, which in this configuration always reports not preempted.
ABI fact: the per-task address limit macro evaluates to the generic task size limit for any supplied task.
Core scheduling teardown and fork helpers are empty in this configuration, while the idle-CPU query forwards to the generic idle test.

Allocation tagging helpers exchange the current tag with a supplied tag and restore a saved tag, with an optional debug check that the tag was not changed unexpectedly; an alternate configuration defines save as returning an empty value and restore as doing nothing.

One variant derives a compact memory identifier by masking off on-CPU and transit marker bits from the stored value, while the fallback variant returns the task CPU. Associated exec and exit hooks are empty in the fallback configuration.

Cache-aware scheduling keeps a small per-CPU record of recent runtime plus an epoch stamp, and a group object that aggregates a pointer to those records, a serializing primitive, epoch and averaging data, scan timing, footprint and ownership info, plus reference lifetime and deferred reclamation support aligned to avoid sharing.
In the disabled configuration the cache group is an empty type and fork, cleanup, exec-mapping and exit hooks are empty operations.
The raw run-queue accessor has architecture-specific and generic per-CPU forms, and the pinned count is maintained as an integer located at a fixed offset from the raw queue base.

Migration control uses a per-task nesting count. The first disable raises the pinned count and sets the count to one; deeper disables only increment. Enables decrement until the last level, which restores the normal CPU mask when it had been narrowed, orders that restoration before clearing the count, and then lowers the pinned count. An alternate configuration defines both operations as empty.
Changes to migration state and the pinned count execute with preemption held, so that stop-task activity and mask restoration cannot interleave with scheduling.
Automatic grouping create, detach, fork, exit and task-exit hooks are all empty operations in this configuration.
Clock helpers report a stable clock, provide empty tick, clear and idle-event operations, and map CPU and local time queries onto the base scheduler clock, including instrumentation-safe forms.
An alternate CPU clock forwards to the per-CPU scheduler clock, and the interrupt-time enable and disable helpers are empty.
ABI fact: dumpability uses zero for off, one for owner-based default, and two for root-like behavior, with differing ptrace capability expectations.
ABI fact: the input-wait hint for frequency updates occupies the lowest bit of the flags word.
Frequency update registration carries a single callback that receives the registration itself plus a timestamp and flags.
Utility mapping scales a frequency value proportionally to utilization over capacity, and a performance mapping inflates utilization by one quarter to add headroom.

Basic accounting copies stored user and system counters to caller outputs and reports no extra adjustment, while guest time is returned directly and scaled accounting either copies stored scaled counters or falls back to the basic copy.

The running group timer lookup returns the signal-level timer only when POSIX CPU timers are active and the task still has sighand state; otherwise it returns empty, and an alternate configuration always returns empty.
Group user, system and execution-time accounting each look up the running timer and add the supplied delta to the corresponding atomic counter, doing nothing when no timer is running.
Previous-time state initialization clears stored user and system deltas and initializes its guard except under native virtual accounting where it is empty.
Stolen-time lookup for a CPU delegates to a paravirtual static call.

Deadline priority holds for values below a configured threshold, deadline task status follows the task priority, earlier deadline comparison uses signed difference semantics, and a deadline entity is implicit when its deadline equals its period.
A predicate reports whether a deadline entity represents a server, and a container helper recovers the owning task while asserting the entity is not a server.
The state dumper forwards a zero filter to the filtered dumper, and the scheduling section marker places annotated code in a dedicated text section.
Execution state bundles a reference count, a dumpability level, an owning user namespace pointer, and a deferred reclamation hook.

ABI fact: scheduler-extension operation names allow up to one hundred twenty eight characters, the default slice equals twenty milliseconds, the bypass slice equals five milliseconds, and the infinite slice is the maximum unsigned sixty four bit value and implies tickless operation.

ABI fact: dispatch queue identifiers reserve the two highest bits as builtin and local-on markers, define small builtin numbers for invalid global local bypass reject and rescue queues, treat local-on as a combination of markers, and carry CPU identity in the low thirty two bits.
Deferred re-enqueue state pairs list linkage with flags, and per-CPU dispatch state pairs a queue pointer with that deferred state.

A dispatch queue combines a serializing primitive with a lockless peek at the head task, ordered list and priority-tree membership, occupancy and sequence counters, an identifier, hash and deferred-free linkage, a back pointer to scheduler state, per-CPU storage, and a reclamation hook.

Extension task state packs one-bit conditions for queued custody runnable-reset sleep-dequeue sub-initialization immediate and protected modes, a three-bit lifecycle progressing from none through begin init ready and enabled to dead, a three-bit re-enqueue reason distinguishing none kfunc immediate preempted and capacity causes, and a high-bit cursor marker.

ABI fact: dispatch membership uses the lowest bit to record priority-queue presence, list nodes reserve the lowest bit for iteration cursors with private cursor data shifted by sixteen, and cursor initialization captures the queue sequence.

Misuse hazards diagnosed by warnings include setting a blocked association to an empty value or for another task, overwriting or clearing with a mismatched mutex, unbalanced migration enable or overflow of the nesting count, and restoring allocation tags after unexpected modification.
ABI fact: each scheduler sub-header defines its own inclusion guard macro to prevent multiple inclusion.
